# Advanced Alchemy — Complete Documentation



> A carefully crafted, thoroughly tested, optimized companion library for SQLAlchemy.

Source: https://docs.advanced-alchemy.litestar.dev/latest/

# Advanced Alchemy

Write clean [SQLAlchemy](https://docs.sqlalchemy.org/en/20/) applications without repeating database boilerplate.

Advanced Alchemy gives your tables ready-made IDs and timestamps, provides ready-to-use [repositories](https://docs.advanced-alchemy.litestar.dev/latest/usage/repositories/index.html) and [services](https://docs.advanced-alchemy.litestar.dev/latest/usage/services.html) for querying and validation, and plugs directly into [Litestar, FastAPI, Starlette, Flask, and Sanic](https://docs.advanced-alchemy.litestar.dev/latest/usage/frameworks/index.html).

Start tables with built-in UUID or integer keys, automatic timestamps, encrypted fields, password hashes, and file storage.

Fetch, filter, paginate, and bulk-upsert records in one call, then convert rows directly into Pydantic or Msgspec schemas.

Automatic per-request database sessions, dependency injection, file uploads, and migration CLIs for Python web frameworks.

Add read-replica routing, automatic query caching, Alembic migrations, and fixture seeding as your application grows.

Source: https://docs.advanced-alchemy.litestar.dev/latest/getting-started.html

# Getting Started

When you build an app with SQLAlchemy from scratch, you end up writing the same plumbing over and over: ID and timestamp columns on every table, `select()` and pagination queries in every endpoint, and session cleanup code for every web request.

Advanced Alchemy handles that repetitive plumbing while keeping plain SQLAlchemy 2.0 front and center:

- **Models** come with ready-made IDs, `created_at` / `updated_at` timestamps, and portable column types.
- **Repositories** give every model `add`, `get`, `list_and_count`, `upsert`, and `delete` methods out of the box.
- **Services** connect your repositories to Pydantic, Msgspec, or dataclass API schemas.
- **Framework plugins** manage database engines and per-request sessions automatically.

## Installation

Install `advanced-alchemy` with your preferred package manager. For the quick example below, we also include `aiosqlite` so it runs in memory with zero database setup:

```bash
uv add advanced-alchemy aiosqlite
```

```bash
pip install advanced-alchemy aiosqlite
```

```bash
pdm add advanced-alchemy aiosqlite
```

```bash
poetry add advanced-alchemy aiosqlite
```

## Your First Model and Repository

Imagine you are building a small blog. Define a `BlogPost` table using `UUIDAuditBase` (which automatically adds a UUID `id` plus `created_at` and `updated_at` columns) and attach a repository to save and query posts:

```python
from sqlalchemy.ext.asyncio import AsyncSession
from sqlalchemy.orm import Mapped
from advanced_alchemy.base import UUIDAuditBase
from advanced_alchemy.repository import SQLAlchemyAsyncRepository

class BlogPost(UUIDAuditBase):
    __tablename__ = "quickstart_post"

    title: Mapped[str]
    published: Mapped[bool] = False

class BlogPostRepository(SQLAlchemyAsyncRepository[BlogPost]):
    model_type = BlogPost

async def run_demo(db_session: AsyncSession) -> None:
    conn = await db_session.connection()
    await conn.run_sync(UUIDAuditBase.metadata.create_all)

    repo = BlogPostRepository(session=db_session)
    await repo.add(BlogPost(title="Hello Advanced Alchemy", published=True))
    await db_session.commit()

    posts, total = await repo.list_and_count(published=True)
    assert total == 1
    assert posts[0].title == "Hello Advanced Alchemy"
```

# Usage Guide

Imagine you are building a blog with **Posts**, **Authors**, and **Tags**. A reader opens your home page, asks for page 2 of published posts, and creates a comment.

Advanced Alchemy organizes that work into three clear steps so your route handlers stay tiny and easy to test:

1. **Models** describe what your tables look like in the database (such as a post’s title, author, and timestamps).
2. **Repositories** run SQL queries for one table—adding rows, filtering, sorting, and paginating without repeating query code.
3. **Services** sit in front of repositories to validate incoming API schemas (Pydantic or Msgspec) and enforce your app’s business rules.

Define tables with automatic UUID or integer primary keys, audit timestamps, JSON, encrypted columns, and file storage.

Add, fetch, filter, paginate, and bulk-upsert records using async or sync sessions.

Keep business rules in one place and convert database rows straight into Pydantic or Msgspec responses.

Connect your services to Litestar, FastAPI, Starlette, Flask, or Sanic with automatic session management.

## Scaling and Day-Two Tools

Once your core tables and routes are running, you can turn on operational features without rewriting your queries:

- [Replica Routing](https://docs.advanced-alchemy.litestar.dev/latest/usage/routing.html) — Send writes to your primary database and spread reads across read replicas.
- [Caching](https://docs.advanced-alchemy.litestar.dev/latest/usage/caching.html) — Cache frequent lookups in Redis or memory and clear stale entries automatically on commit.
- [CLI & Migrations](https://docs.advanced-alchemy.litestar.dev/latest/usage/cli.html) — Generate and apply Alembic schema migrations from the terminal.
- [Database Seeding](https://docs.advanced-alchemy.litestar.dev/latest/usage/database_seeding.html) — Load starter data from JSON or CSV files.

Source: https://docs.advanced-alchemy.litestar.dev/latest/usage/modeling/index.html

# Data Modeling

Every database table needs a few essentials: a primary key, clear column types, and usually `created_at` and `updated_at` timestamps so you know when rows changed.

Advanced Alchemy gives you ready-to-use base classes and portable column types so you only write the columns unique to your app.

Pick a base class for integer or UUID keys, add URL slugs, and wire relationships between tables.

Share columns across related models using single-table, joined-table, or concrete-table layouts.

Store UTC timestamps, UUIDs, JSON documents, and vector embeddings that work across SQLite and production SQL engines.

Encrypt sensitive strings, hash passwords, verify one-time codes, and attach uploaded files to rows.

Source: https://docs.advanced-alchemy.litestar.dev/latest/usage/modeling/basics.html

# Modeling Basics

When you create a new table—like `BlogPost` or `Author`—you almost always want an `id` column and `created_at` / `updated_at` timestamps. Instead of copying those columns onto every model, inherit from one of Advanced Alchemy’s base classes.

## Choosing a Base Class

Pick the base class that matches how you want row IDs generated. Every `*Base` class also has an `*AuditBase` twin that adds automatic `created_at` and `updated_at` UTC timestamps:

| Base Class | Best When You Want |
| --- | --- |
| `UUIDv7Base` / `UUIDv7AuditBase` | Time-sorted UUID primary keys that index well and stay safe to expose in URLs. |
| `UUIDBase` / `UUIDAuditBase` | Random UUIDv4 primary keys. |
| `BigIntBase` / `BigIntAuditBase` | Auto-incrementing 64-bit integer IDs (`1, 2, 3...`) that also work in SQLite tests. |
| `IdentityBase` / `IdentityAuditBase` | SQL standard `GENERATED BY DEFAULT AS IDENTITY` integer primary keys. |
| `NanoIDBase` / `NanoIDAuditBase` | Short, URL-friendly string IDs. |
| `DefaultBase` | A clean blank slate when you want to define your own primary key or composite key. |

Here is a blog post table with an auto-incrementing integer ID and automatic `created_at` / `updated_at` columns:

```python
import datetime
from typing import Optional
from sqlalchemy.orm import Mapped, mapped_column
from advanced_alchemy.base import BigIntAuditBase

class BasicBlogPost(BigIntAuditBase):
    __tablename__ = "basic_blog_post"

    title: Mapped[str] = mapped_column(index=True)
    content: Mapped[str]
    published: Mapped[bool] = mapped_column(default=False)
    published_at: Mapped[Optional[datetime.datetime]] = mapped_column(default=None)
```

```python
import datetime
from sqlalchemy.orm import Mapped, mapped_column
from advanced_alchemy.base import BigIntAuditBase

class BasicBlogPost(BigIntAuditBase):
    __tablename__ = "basic_blog_post"

    title: Mapped[str] = mapped_column(index=True)
    content: Mapped[str]
    published: Mapped[bool] = mapped_column(default=False)
    published_at: Mapped[datetime.datetime | None] = mapped_column(default=None)
```

> **Tip**: Base classes and mixins automatically keep your physical table columns tidy: `id` comes first, your custom columns sit in the middle, and audit timestamps sit at the end.

## Many-to-Many Relationships

Suppose one blog post can have several topics, and one topic belongs to many posts. Join them with a link table attached to `orm_registry.metadata`, and mix in `SlugKey` to give each topic a URL-friendly `slug` column:

```python
from sqlalchemy import Column, ForeignKey, Table
from sqlalchemy.orm import Mapped, mapped_column, relationship
from advanced_alchemy.base import BigIntAuditBase, orm_registry
from advanced_alchemy.mixins import SlugKey

blog_post_topic = Table(
    "blog_post_topic",
    orm_registry.metadata,
    Column("post_id", ForeignKey("tagged_blog_post.id", ondelete="CASCADE"), primary_key=True),
    Column("topic_id", ForeignKey("blog_topic.id", ondelete="CASCADE"), primary_key=True),
)

class TaggedBlogPost(BigIntAuditBase):
    __tablename__ = "tagged_blog_post"

    title: Mapped[str] = mapped_column(index=True)
    topics: Mapped[list["BlogTopic"]] = relationship(
        secondary=blog_post_topic,
        back_populates="posts",
        lazy="selectin",
    )

class BlogTopic(BigIntAuditBase, SlugKey):
    __tablename__ = "blog_topic"

    name: Mapped[str] = mapped_column(unique=True, index=True)
    posts: Mapped[list["TaggedBlogPost"]] = relationship(
        secondary=blog_post_topic,
        back_populates="topics",
        lazy="selectin",
    )
```

## Preventing Duplicate Rows

When users tag a post with `"Python"` and `"python"`, you usually want both to point to the same tag row instead of crashing with a duplicate-key error. Mix in `UniqueMixin` and tell it how to recognize an existing record:

```python
from typing import Optional
from collections.abc import Hashable
from sqlalchemy.orm import Mapped, mapped_column
from sqlalchemy.sql.elements import ColumnElement
from advanced_alchemy.base import BigIntAuditBase
from advanced_alchemy.mixins import SlugKey, UniqueMixin
from advanced_alchemy.utils.text import slugify

class UniqueTopic(BigIntAuditBase, SlugKey, UniqueMixin):
    __tablename__ = "unique_topic"

    name: Mapped[str] = mapped_column(unique=True, index=True)

    @classmethod
    def unique_hash(cls, name: str, slug: Optional[str] = None) -> Hashable:
        del slug
        return slugify(name)

    @classmethod
    def unique_filter(cls, name: str, slug: Optional[str] = None) -> ColumnElement[bool]:
        del slug
        return cls.slug == slugify(name)
```

```python
from collections.abc import Hashable
from sqlalchemy.orm import Mapped, mapped_column
from sqlalchemy.sql.elements import ColumnElement
from advanced_alchemy.base import BigIntAuditBase
from advanced_alchemy.mixins import SlugKey, UniqueMixin
from advanced_alchemy.utils.text import slugify

class UniqueTopic(BigIntAuditBase, SlugKey, UniqueMixin):
    __tablename__ = "unique_topic"

    name: Mapped[str] = mapped_column(unique=True, index=True)

    @classmethod
    def unique_hash(cls, name: str, slug: str | None = None) -> Hashable:
        del slug
        return slugify(name)

    @classmethod
    def unique_filter(cls, name: str, slug: str | None = None) -> ColumnElement[bool]:
        del slug
        return cls.slug == slugify(name)
```

## Custom Keys and Dataclass Models

Need to supply your own primary key (such as an external SKU code) or prefer Python dataclass syntax? Combine `DefaultBase` with `AuditColumns` or SQLAlchemy’s `MappedAsDataclass`:

```python
from sqlalchemy.orm import Mapped, mapped_column
from advanced_alchemy.base import DefaultBase
from advanced_alchemy.mixins import AuditColumns

class ImportedProduct(DefaultBase, AuditColumns):
    __tablename__ = "imported_product"

    id: Mapped[str] = mapped_column(primary_key=True)
    name: Mapped[str]
```

```python
from typing import Optional
from sqlalchemy.orm import Mapped, MappedAsDataclass, mapped_column
from advanced_alchemy.base import DefaultBase

class DataclassAuthor(MappedAsDataclass, DefaultBase):
    __tablename__ = "dataclass_author"

    id: Mapped[int] = mapped_column(primary_key=True, init=False)
    name: Mapped[str]
    bio: Mapped[Optional[str]] = mapped_column(default=None)
```

```python
from sqlalchemy.orm import Mapped, MappedAsDataclass, mapped_column
from advanced_alchemy.base import DefaultBase

class DataclassAuthor(MappedAsDataclass, DefaultBase):
    __tablename__ = "dataclass_author"

    id: Mapped[int] = mapped_column(primary_key=True, init=False)
    name: Mapped[str]
    bio: Mapped[str | None] = mapped_column(default=None)
```

See [base](https://docs.advanced-alchemy.litestar.dev/latest/reference/base.html) and [mixins](https://docs.advanced-alchemy.litestar.dev/latest/reference/mixins/index.html) for the full list of base classes and mixins.

Source: https://docs.advanced-alchemy.litestar.dev/latest/usage/modeling/inheritance.html

# Inheritance Patterns

Sometimes several models share most of their fields—for example, **Managers** and **Engineers** are both **Employees**, or **Articles** and **Videos** are both **Posts**.

SQLAlchemy supports three ways to lay out shared models in the database, and Advanced Alchemy’s base classes and repositories work with all three:

- **Single Table**: Everything lives in **one table** with a `type` column. Fastest to query when subclasses only add a few optional columns.
- **Joined Table**: Shared fields live in a **parent table**, and extra fields live in **child tables** linked by a foreign key. Best when subclasses have many required columns.
- **Concrete Table**: An abstract Python base class shares column definitions, while each subclass gets its own **separate table**.

## Comparing the Layouts

```python
from typing import Optional
from sqlalchemy.orm import Mapped
from advanced_alchemy.base import UUIDAuditBase

class Employee(UUIDAuditBase):
    __tablename__ = "employee"
    name: Mapped[str]
    type: Mapped[str]

    __mapper_args__ = {
        "polymorphic_on": "type",
        "polymorphic_identity": "employee",
    }

class Manager(Employee):
    __mapper_args__ = {"polymorphic_identity": "manager"}
    department: Mapped[Optional[str]]

class Engineer(Employee):
    __mapper_args__ = {"polymorphic_identity": "engineer"}
    primary_language: Mapped[Optional[str]]
```

```python
from sqlalchemy.orm import Mapped
from advanced_alchemy.base import UUIDAuditBase

class Employee(UUIDAuditBase):
    __tablename__ = "employee"
    name: Mapped[str]
    type: Mapped[str]

    __mapper_args__ = {
        "polymorphic_on": "type",
        "polymorphic_identity": "employee",
    }

class Manager(Employee):
    __mapper_args__ = {"polymorphic_identity": "manager"}
    department: Mapped[str | None]

class Engineer(Employee):
    __mapper_args__ = {"polymorphic_identity": "engineer"}
    primary_language: Mapped[str | None]
```

```python
from uuid import UUID
from sqlalchemy import ForeignKey
from sqlalchemy.orm import Mapped, mapped_column
from advanced_alchemy.base import UUIDAuditBase

class Person(UUIDAuditBase):
    __tablename__ = "person"
    name: Mapped[str]
    type: Mapped[str]

    __mapper_args__ = {
        "polymorphic_on": "type",
        "polymorphic_identity": "person",
    }

class Staff(Person):
    __tablename__ = "staff"
    id: Mapped[UUID] = mapped_column(ForeignKey("person.id"), primary_key=True)
    badge_number: Mapped[str]

    __mapper_args__ = {"polymorphic_identity": "staff"}
```

```python
from sqlalchemy.orm import Mapped
from advanced_alchemy.base import UUIDAuditBase

class Vehicle(UUIDAuditBase):
    __abstract__ = True
    name: Mapped[str]

class Car(Vehicle):
    __tablename__ = "car"
    engine_type: Mapped[str]

class Bicycle(Vehicle):
    __tablename__ = "bicycle"
    has_basket: Mapped[bool]
```

## Querying Inherited Models

Attach a repository to the parent model when you want all subtypes back together, or attach one to a child model when you only want rows of that specific subtype:

```python
from sqlalchemy.ext.asyncio import AsyncSession
from advanced_alchemy.repository import SQLAlchemyAsyncRepository

class EmployeeRepository(SQLAlchemyAsyncRepository[Employee]):
    model_type = Employee

class ManagerRepository(SQLAlchemyAsyncRepository[Manager]):
    model_type = Manager

async def list_staff(db_session: AsyncSession) -> tuple[list[Employee], list[Manager]]:
    all_employees = await EmployeeRepository(session=db_session).get_many()
    only_managers = await ManagerRepository(session=db_session).get_many()
    return all_employees, only_managers
```

Source: https://docs.advanced-alchemy.litestar.dev/latest/usage/modeling/sqlmodel.html

# SQLModel Integration

If your team already writes tables with [SQLModel](https://sqlmodel.tiangolo.com/), you can plug those models straight into Advanced Alchemy repositories without rewriting your model classes.

## Defining and Querying a SQLModel Table

Mark your SQLModel class with `table=True` and point a repository at it just like any SQLAlchemy model:

```python
from typing import Optional
from sqlalchemy.ext.asyncio import AsyncSession, async_sessionmaker, create_async_engine
from sqlmodel import Field, SQLModel
from advanced_alchemy.repository import SQLAlchemyAsyncRepository

class Hero(SQLModel, table=True):
    id: Optional[int] = Field(default=None, primary_key=True)
    name: str
    secret_name: str
    age: Optional[int] = None

class HeroRepository(SQLAlchemyAsyncRepository[Hero]):
    model_type = Hero

async def create_and_list_heroes() -> list[Hero]:
    engine = create_async_engine("sqlite+aiosqlite:///:memory:")
    session_factory = async_sessionmaker(engine, expire_on_commit=False, class_=AsyncSession)

    async with engine.begin() as conn:
        await conn.run_sync(SQLModel.metadata.create_all)

    try:
        async with session_factory() as session:
            repo = HeroRepository(session=session)
            await repo.add(Hero(name="Spider-Man", secret_name="Peter Parker"))
            await session.commit()
            return await repo.get_many()
    finally:
        await engine.dispose()
```

```python
from sqlalchemy.ext.asyncio import AsyncSession, async_sessionmaker, create_async_engine
from sqlmodel import Field, SQLModel
from advanced_alchemy.repository import SQLAlchemyAsyncRepository

class Hero(SQLModel, table=True):
    id: int | None = Field(default=None, primary_key=True)
    name: str
    secret_name: str
    age: int | None = None

class HeroRepository(SQLAlchemyAsyncRepository[Hero]):
    model_type = Hero

async def create_and_list_heroes() -> list[Hero]:
    engine = create_async_engine("sqlite+aiosqlite:///:memory:")
    session_factory = async_sessionmaker(engine, expire_on_commit=False, class_=AsyncSession)

    async with engine.begin() as conn:
        await conn.run_sync(SQLModel.metadata.create_all)

    try:
        async with session_factory() as session:
            repo = HeroRepository(session=session)
            await repo.add(Hero(name="Spider-Man", secret_name="Peter Parker"))
            await session.commit()
            return await repo.get_many()
    finally:
        await engine.dispose()
```

## Good to Know

SQLModel uses its own `SQLModel.metadata` registry instead of Advanced Alchemy’s `orm_registry`. Pass `metadata=SQLModel.metadata` in your framework config so migrations and table creation helpers target your SQLModel tables.

Source: https://docs.advanced-alchemy.litestar.dev/latest/usage/modeling/types.html

# Portable Column Types

Different SQL databases use different column types for UUIDs, UTC timestamps, JSON, and AI vector embeddings—especially when you test against SQLite locally and deploy to PostgreSQL, MySQL, or Oracle in production.

Advanced Alchemy’s column types automatically pick the best native database type on each engine while keeping your Python types consistent.

## Common Column Types at a Glance

| Column Type | What It Does |
| --- | --- |
| `DateTimeUTC` | Converts datetimes to UTC before saving, returns timezone-aware UTC datetimes on read, and supports configurable fractional-second precision (`DateTimeUTC(fsp=6)`). |
| `GUID` | Stores Python `UUID` objects natively on PostgreSQL, CockroachDB, DuckDB, MSSQL, and Oracle, or compactly on SQLite/MySQL. |
| `BigIntIdentity` | Uses 64-bit `BIGINT` in production and `INTEGER` on SQLite so auto-incrementing IDs work in local tests. |
| `JsonB` | Uses fast binary JSON on PostgreSQL, CockroachDB, and Oracle, and standard `JSON` everywhere else. |
| `Vector(dim=...)` | Stores float embeddings for similarity search (`pgvector`, Oracle 23ai+, CockroachDB, DuckDB, and SQLite fallback). |

## Examples by Type

```python
from datetime import datetime
from sqlalchemy.orm import Mapped, mapped_column
from advanced_alchemy.base import BigIntBase, UUIDBase, create_registry
from advanced_alchemy.types import DateTimeUTC, JsonB

class AuditEvent(BigIntBase):
    __tablename__ = "audit_event"

    occurred_at: Mapped[datetime] = mapped_column(DateTimeUTC(fsp=6))
    metadata_payload: Mapped[dict[str, str]] = mapped_column(JsonB)

class PrecisionBase(UUIDBase):
    __abstract__ = True
    registry = create_registry(custom_annotation_map={datetime: DateTimeUTC(fsp=6)})
```

```python
from uuid import UUID
from sqlalchemy.orm import Mapped, mapped_column
from advanced_alchemy.base import DefaultBase
from advanced_alchemy.types import BigIntIdentity, GUID

class LedgerEntry(DefaultBase):
    __tablename__ = "ledger_entry"

    id: Mapped[int] = mapped_column(BigIntIdentity, primary_key=True)
    external_ref: Mapped[UUID] = mapped_column(GUID, index=True)
```

```python
from sqlalchemy.orm import Mapped, mapped_column
from advanced_alchemy.base import UUIDv7Base
from advanced_alchemy.types import Vector

class DocumentChunk(UUIDv7Base):
    __tablename__ = "document_chunk"

    embedding: Mapped[list[float]] = mapped_column(Vector(dim=3))
```

> **Note**: On MySQL/MariaDB and Oracle, SQLAlchemy’s default `DateTime(timezone=True)` stores whole seconds only. Pass `DateTimeUTC(fsp=6)` (or set `custom_annotation_map={datetime: DateTimeUTC(fsp=6)}` via [`create_registry()`](https://docs.advanced-alchemy.litestar.dev/latest/reference/base.html#advanced_alchemy.base.create_registry)) to preserve microseconds, or pass `DateTimeUTC(fsp=0)` to keep legacy whole-second DDL without migration churn. In v2.0, `fsp=6` becomes the default.

# Security and File Storage Types

Most apps eventually need to store sensitive values—API keys, user passwords, two-factor login codes—or attach uploaded files like avatars and PDF reports to a database row.

Advanced Alchemy provides dedicated column types so sensitive values are never stored in plain text and uploaded files stay in sync with your database transactions.

## Encrypted Text and Password Hashing

Use `EncryptedString` or `EncryptedText` when your app needs to decrypt a secret later (like an API token), and `PasswordHash` when storing one-way user passwords:

```python
from sqlalchemy.orm import Mapped, mapped_column
from advanced_alchemy.base import BigIntBase
from advanced_alchemy.types import EncryptedString, EncryptedText

class SecretRecord(BigIntBase):
    __tablename__ = "secret_record"

    api_token: Mapped[str] = mapped_column(EncryptedString(key="my-secret-key"))
    private_notes: Mapped[str] = mapped_column(EncryptedText(key="my-secret-key"))
```

```python
from sqlalchemy.orm import Mapped, mapped_column
from advanced_alchemy.base import BigIntBase
from advanced_alchemy.types import HashedPassword, PasswordHash
from advanced_alchemy.types.password_hash.argon2 import Argon2Hasher

hasher = Argon2Hasher()

class AccountRecord(BigIntBase):
    __tablename__ = "account_record"

    password: Mapped[str] = mapped_column(PasswordHash(backend=hasher))

stored = HashedPassword(hasher.hash("s3cret-passphrase"), hasher)
verified, _ = stored.verify_and_update("s3cret-passphrase")
assert verified is True
```

## Two-Factor Secrets and One-Time Codes

For multi-factor login flows, `TOTPSecret` encrypts authenticator app seeds (Google Authenticator, 1Password), while `OneTimeCode` hashes short-lived email or SMS verification codes and tracks retry limits:

```python
from sqlalchemy.orm import Mapped, mapped_column
from advanced_alchemy.base import BigIntBase
from advanced_alchemy.types import TOTPProvider, TOTPSecret, generate_totp_secret

class MfaEnrollment(BigIntBase):
    __tablename__ = "mfa_enrollment"

    seed: Mapped[str] = mapped_column(TOTPSecret(key="my-secret-key", issuer="ACME"))

provider = TOTPProvider(generate_totp_secret(), issuer="ACME")
uri = provider.provisioning_uri(name="alice@example.com")
assert uri.startswith("otpauth://totp/")
```

```python
from typing import Any
from sqlalchemy.orm import Mapped, mapped_column
from advanced_alchemy.base import BigIntBase
from advanced_alchemy.types import HashedOneTimeCode, OneTimeCode, generate_one_time_code
from advanced_alchemy.types.password_hash.argon2 import Argon2Hasher

otp_hasher = Argon2Hasher()

class LoginCode(BigIntBase):
    __tablename__ = "login_code"

    code: Mapped[Any] = mapped_column(
        OneTimeCode(backend=otp_hasher, ttl_seconds=600, max_attempts=3),
    )

raw_code = generate_one_time_code()
otp = HashedOneTimeCode(otp_hasher.hash(raw_code), otp_hasher, max_attempts=3)
ok, otp = otp.redeem(raw_code)
assert ok is True and otp.is_used is True
```

## File and Object Storage

Instead of storing large binary blobs inside SQL tables, `StoredObject` saves lightweight file metadata in your table and writes the file bytes to local disk, S3, Google Cloud Storage, or Azure via `storages`:

```python
from pathlib import Path
import tempfile
from typing import Optional
from sqlalchemy.orm import Mapped, mapped_column
from advanced_alchemy.base import UUIDBase
from advanced_alchemy.types import FileObject, FileObjectList, StoredObject, storages

tmp_storage = tempfile.mkdtemp()
storages.register_backend(f"file://{Path(tmp_storage)}", key="documents")

class DocumentRecord(UUIDBase):
    __tablename__ = "document_record"

    attachment: Mapped[Optional[FileObject]] = mapped_column(
        StoredObject(backend="documents"),
        nullable=True,
    )
    images: Mapped[Optional[FileObjectList]] = mapped_column(
        StoredObject(backend="documents", multiple=True),
        nullable=True,
    )

file_obj = FileObject(backend="documents", filename="report.txt", metadata={"category": "report"})
file_obj.update_metadata({"priority": "high"})
storages.clear_backends()
```

```python
from pathlib import Path
import tempfile
from sqlalchemy.orm import Mapped, mapped_column
from advanced_alchemy.base import UUIDBase
from advanced_alchemy.types import FileObject, FileObjectList, StoredObject, storages

tmp_storage = tempfile.mkdtemp()
storages.register_backend(f"file://{Path(tmp_storage)}", key="documents")

class DocumentRecord(UUIDBase):
    __tablename__ = "document_record"

    attachment: Mapped[FileObject | None] = mapped_column(
        StoredObject(backend="documents"),
        nullable=True,
    )
    images: Mapped[FileObjectList | None] = mapped_column(
        StoredObject(backend="documents", multiple=True),
        nullable=True,
    )

file_obj = FileObject(backend="documents", filename="report.txt", metadata={"category": "report"})
file_obj.update_metadata({"priority": "high"})
storages.clear_backends()
```

See [Litestar File and Object Storage](https://docs.advanced-alchemy.litestar.dev/latest/usage/frameworks/litestar_storage.html) and [FastAPI File Storage and Multi-Binds](https://docs.advanced-alchemy.litestar.dev/latest/usage/frameworks/fastapi_storage.html) for complete file-upload web examples.

Source: https://docs.advanced-alchemy.litestar.dev/latest/usage/repositories/index.html

# Repositories

Without a repository, every web route ends up repeating the same SQLAlchemy query code: building a `select()`, adding `where()` clauses, counting total rows for pagination, and handling `NoResultFound` errors.

A **Repository** wraps one table model and gives you ready-made, type-checked methods—`add`, `get`, `get_many`, `list_and_count`, `upsert_many`, and `delete`—so your routes read like plain English.

Add, fetch, update, bulk-upsert, and delete records with async or sync repositories.

Search text, filter by IDs or dates, and return paginated results with total counts.

Work with composite primary keys, row-level locks, and bulk conditional deletes.

Source: https://docs.advanced-alchemy.litestar.dev/latest/usage/repositories/basics.html

# Repository Basics

Think of a **Repository** as a dedicated helper for one database table. Instead of writing raw SQLAlchemy `select()` and `session.add()` calls throughout your app, you point a repository at your `Post` model once and call clear methods like `repo.add(post)`, `repo.get(post_id)`, or `repo.get_many()`.

## Choosing a Repository Class

Every async repository has an identical synchronous version—pick async when using `AsyncSession` and sync when using `Session`:

| Repository Type | When to Use It |
| --- | --- |
| `SQLAlchemyAsyncRepository` / `SQLAlchemySyncRepository` | Everyday tables: create, read, update, delete, filter, paginate, and bulk upsert. |
| `SQLAlchemyAsyncSlugRepository` / `SQLAlchemySyncSlugRepository` | Tables with URL slugs (like `/posts/hello-world`): generates unique slugs and looks up rows by slug. |
| `SQLAlchemyAsyncQueryRepository` / `SQLAlchemySyncQueryRepository` | Custom `SELECT` queries, joins, and `GROUP BY` summaries that don’t map to a single model. |

## Creating and Reading Rows

Suppose our blog has `Post` and `Tag` tables. Subclass `SQLAlchemyAsyncRepository` and set `model_type = Post`:

```python
from sqlalchemy.ext.asyncio import AsyncSession
from sqlalchemy.orm import Mapped, mapped_column
from advanced_alchemy.base import BigIntAuditBase
from advanced_alchemy.mixins import SlugKey
from advanced_alchemy.repository import SQLAlchemyAsyncRepository

class Post(BigIntAuditBase):
    __tablename__ = "repo_basics_post"

    title: Mapped[str]
    content: Mapped[str]
    published: Mapped[bool] = mapped_column(default=False)

class Tag(BigIntAuditBase, SlugKey):
    __tablename__ = "repo_basics_tag"

    name: Mapped[str]

class PostRepository(SQLAlchemyAsyncRepository[Post]):
    model_type = Post

async def create_and_fetch_post(db_session: AsyncSession) -> Post:
    repo = PostRepository(session=db_session)
    saved = await repo.add(
        Post(title="Getting Started", content="Repositories keep queries simple."),
        auto_commit=True,
    )
    return await repo.get(saved.id)
```

## Saving, Updating, and Deleting in Bulk

When importing a batch of drafts or publishing ten posts at once, looping one query at a time is slow. Use the `*_many` methods to handle whole batches in a single step:

```python
from collections.abc import Sequence
from sqlalchemy.ext.asyncio import AsyncSession

async def create_drafts(
    db_session: AsyncSession,
    drafts: list[tuple[str, str]],
) -> Sequence[Post]:
    repo = PostRepository(session=db_session)
    return await repo.add_many(
        [Post(title=title, content=body) for title, body in drafts],
        auto_commit=True,
    )
```

```python
from sqlalchemy.ext.asyncio import AsyncSession

async def publish_posts(db_session: AsyncSession, post_ids: list[int]) -> list[Post]:
    repo = PostRepository(session=db_session)
    posts = await repo.get_many(Post.id.in_(post_ids), published=False)
    for post in posts:
        post.published = True
    return await repo.update_many(posts, auto_commit=True)
```

```python
from collections.abc import Sequence
from sqlalchemy.ext.asyncio import AsyncSession

async def remove_posts(db_session: AsyncSession, post_ids: list[int]) -> Sequence[Post]:
    repo = PostRepository(session=db_session)
    return await repo.delete_many(post_ids, auto_commit=True)
```

## Syncing External Data with Upserts

Imagine syncing posts from an external CMS: some posts are brand new, and others are updates to rows already in your database.

`upsert_many` inserts new rows and updates matching ones in one call. Behind the scenes, it uses your database’s native upsert command (such as `ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE` on PostgreSQL/SQLite or `MERGE` on Oracle/SQL Server) whenever `match_fields` points to a unique column, and safely falls back to a standard lookup-and-save flow otherwise:

```python
from collections.abc import Sequence
from sqlalchemy.ext.asyncio import AsyncSession

async def sync_imported_posts(db_session: AsyncSession, incoming: list[Post]) -> Sequence[Post]:
    repo = PostRepository(session=db_session)
    return await repo.upsert_many(
        incoming,
        match_fields=["id"],
        auto_commit=True,
    )
```

## URL Slugs and Summary Queries

Need to look up tags by URL slug (like `/tags/python`) or run a custom `GROUP BY` count? Use the slug or query repository:

```python
from sqlalchemy.ext.asyncio import AsyncSession
from advanced_alchemy.repository import SQLAlchemyAsyncSlugRepository

class TagRepository(SQLAlchemyAsyncSlugRepository[Tag]):
    model_type = Tag

async def find_tag(db_session: AsyncSession, slug: str) -> Tag:
    repo = TagRepository(session=db_session)
    return await repo.get_by_slug(slug)
```

```python
from typing import Any
from sqlalchemy import Row, func, select
from sqlalchemy.ext.asyncio import AsyncSession
from advanced_alchemy.repository import SQLAlchemyAsyncQueryRepository

async def count_posts_by_status(db_session: AsyncSession) -> list[Row[Any]]:
    query_repo = SQLAlchemyAsyncQueryRepository(session=db_session)
    return await query_repo.get_many(
        select(Post.published, func.count(Post.id)).group_by(Post.published),
    )
```

- [Filtering and Pagination](https://docs.advanced-alchemy.litestar.dev/latest/usage/repositories/filtering.html) — Search text, filter by lists or null values, and paginate results.
- [repositories](https://docs.advanced-alchemy.litestar.dev/latest/reference/repository.html) — Complete repository API reference.

Source: https://docs.advanced-alchemy.litestar.dev/latest/usage/repositories/filtering.html

# Filtering and Pagination

Suppose a reader visits your blog and searches for `"python"`, filters to published articles from the past week, and views 20 posts per page.

Instead of manually conditionally appending `.where()` and `.limit()` clauses in every route, you can pass both plain SQLAlchemy expressions and ready-made filter objects directly into your repository calls.

## Example Setup

```python
import datetime
from typing import Optional
from sqlalchemy.orm import Mapped, mapped_column
from advanced_alchemy.base import BigIntAuditBase
from advanced_alchemy.repository import SQLAlchemyAsyncRepository

class FilteringPost(BigIntAuditBase):
    __tablename__ = "filtering_post"

    title: Mapped[str]
    content: Mapped[str]
    published: Mapped[bool] = mapped_column(default=False)
    published_at: Mapped[Optional[datetime.datetime]] = mapped_column(default=None)

class FilteringPostRepository(SQLAlchemyAsyncRepository[FilteringPost]):
    model_type = FilteringPost
```

```python
import datetime
from sqlalchemy.orm import Mapped, mapped_column
from advanced_alchemy.base import BigIntAuditBase
from advanced_alchemy.repository import SQLAlchemyAsyncRepository

class FilteringPost(BigIntAuditBase):
    __tablename__ = "filtering_post"

    title: Mapped[str]
    content: Mapped[str]
    published: Mapped[bool] = mapped_column(default=False)
    published_at: Mapped[datetime.datetime | None] = mapped_column(default=None)

class FilteringPostRepository(SQLAlchemyAsyncRepository[FilteringPost]):
    model_type = FilteringPost
```

## Plain SQLAlchemy Conditions

For straightforward checks inside Python code, pass normal SQLAlchemy column comparisons straight to `get_many` or `get_many_and_count`:

```python
async def get_recent_posts(db_session: AsyncSession) -> list[FilteringPost]:
    cutoff = datetime.datetime.now(tz=datetime.timezone.utc) - datetime.timedelta(days=7)
    repo = FilteringPostRepository(session=db_session)
    return await repo.get_many(
        FilteringPost.published.is_(True),
        FilteringPost.created_at >= cutoff,
    )
```

## Built-In Filter Helpers

When building web endpoints with optional query parameters, Advanced Alchemy’s filter helpers turn user input into safe SQL conditions:

```python
async def search_posts(db_session: AsyncSession, query: str) -> list[FilteringPost]:
    repo = FilteringPostRepository(session=db_session)
    return await repo.get_many(
        SearchFilter(field_name="title", value=query, ignore_case=True),
    )

literal_discount = SearchFilter(
    field_name="title",
    value="50% off",
    escape_wildcards=True,
)
```

```python
async def get_selected_posts(
    db_session: AsyncSession,
    post_ids: list[int],
) -> list[FilteringPost]:
    repo = FilteringPostRepository(session=db_session)
    return await repo.get_many(
        CollectionFilter(field_name="id", values=post_ids),
    )
```

```python
async def list_drafts_and_published(
    db_session: AsyncSession,
) -> tuple[list[FilteringPost], list[FilteringPost]]:
    repo = FilteringPostRepository(session=db_session)
    drafts = await repo.get_many(NullFilter(field_name="published_at"))
    live = await repo.get_many(NotNullFilter(field_name="published_at"))
    return drafts, live
```

> **Tip**: Set `escape_wildcards=True` on `SearchFilter` when searching text that may contain literal `%` or `_` characters (such as `"50% off"`) on databases that support SQL `ESCAPE`.

## Paginating Results

Combine `LimitOffset` with `get_many_and_count` to get both the current page of rows and the total matching row count for your UI’s page switcher:

```python
async def get_posts_page(
    db_session: AsyncSession,
    page: int = 1,
    page_size: int = 20,
) -> tuple[list[FilteringPost], int]:
    repo = FilteringPostRepository(session=db_session)
    offset = (page - 1) * page_size
    return await repo.get_many_and_count(LimitOffset(offset=offset, limit=page_size))
```

## Naming URL Query Parameters

In Litestar and FastAPI, filter dependencies use camelCase query parameters by default (`?pageSize=10&searchString=python`). Set `alias_generator="snake_case"` in `FilterConfig` when your API prefers `?page_size=10&search_string=python`:

```python
from advanced_alchemy.utils.dependencies import FilterConfig

snake_case_filters: FilterConfig = {
    "pagination_type": "limit_offset",
    "search": "title",
    "sort_field": "created_at",
    "alias_generator": "snake_case",
}
```

If you use [read replicas](https://docs.advanced-alchemy.litestar.dev/latest/usage/routing.html), any read or count call can also target a named replica pool with `bind_group="analytics"`:

```python
async def list_for_reporting(db_session: AsyncSession) -> list[FilteringPost]:
    repo = FilteringPostRepository(session=db_session)
    return await repo.get_many(bind_group="analytics")
```

Source: https://docs.advanced-alchemy.litestar.dev/latest/usage/repositories/advanced.html

# Advanced Repository

Most tables have a single `id` column and simple single-row updates. When you run into trickier real-world cases—join tables with two-part keys, concurrent checkout updates, or clearing old drafts in one query—repositories handle them cleanly.

## Composite Primary Keys

Some tables identify a row by **two columns together** rather than a single `id`—for example, a `UserRole` table keyed by `(user_id, role_id)`.

You can pass composite keys to `get` or `delete_many` as a dictionary (recommended because column names are explicit) or as an ordered tuple:

```python
from sqlalchemy import ForeignKey
from sqlalchemy.orm import Mapped, mapped_column
from advanced_alchemy.base import BigIntBase, DefaultBase
from advanced_alchemy.repository import SQLAlchemyAsyncRepository

class AdvancedUser(BigIntBase):
    __tablename__ = "advanced_user_account"
    username: Mapped[str]

class AdvancedRole(BigIntBase):
    __tablename__ = "advanced_role"
    name: Mapped[str]

class AdvancedUserRole(DefaultBase):
    __tablename__ = "advanced_user_role"

    user_id: Mapped[int] = mapped_column(ForeignKey("advanced_user_account.id"), primary_key=True)
    role_id: Mapped[int] = mapped_column(ForeignKey("advanced_role.id"), primary_key=True)
    permissions: Mapped[str] = mapped_column(default="member")

class AdvancedPost(BigIntBase):
    __tablename__ = "advanced_post"
    title: Mapped[str]
    published: Mapped[bool] = mapped_column(default=False)

class AdvancedUserRoleRepository(SQLAlchemyAsyncRepository[AdvancedUserRole]):
    model_type = AdvancedUserRole

class AdvancedUserRepository(SQLAlchemyAsyncRepository[AdvancedUser]):
    model_type = AdvancedUser

class AdvancedPostRepository(SQLAlchemyAsyncRepository[AdvancedPost]):
    model_type = AdvancedPost
```

```python
async def get_role_by_dict(
    db_session: AsyncSession,
    user_id: int,
    role_id: int,
) -> AdvancedUserRole:
    repo = AdvancedUserRoleRepository(session=db_session)
    return await repo.get({"user_id": user_id, "role_id": role_id})
```

```python
async def get_and_remove_roles(
    db_session: AsyncSession,
    user_id: int,
    role_id: int,
) -> Sequence[AdvancedUserRole]:
    repo = AdvancedUserRoleRepository(session=db_session)
    _ = await repo.get((user_id, role_id))
    return await repo.delete_many([{"user_id": user_id, "role_id": role_id}])
```

## Row Locking

Imagine two requests trying to deduct credits from the same user account at the exact same instant. Passing `with_for_update=True` locks that row in the database until your transaction finishes so the second request waits its turn:

```python
async def lock_user_for_update(db_session: AsyncSession, user_id: int) -> AdvancedUser:
    repo = AdvancedUserRepository(session=db_session)
    return await repo.get_one(id=user_id, with_for_update=True)

async def lock_user_without_waiting(db_session: AsyncSession, user_id: int) -> AdvancedUser:
    repo = AdvancedUserRepository(session=db_session)
    return await repo.get_one(
        id=user_id,
        with_for_update={"nowait": True, "of": AdvancedUser.id},
    )
```

## Deleting Rows by Condition

Need to purge every unpublished draft in one query without loading each post into Python first? Call `delete_where`:

```python
async def purge_unpublished_drafts(db_session: AsyncSession) -> Sequence[AdvancedPost]:
    repo = AdvancedPostRepository(session=db_session)
    return await repo.delete_where(AdvancedPost.published.is_(False))
```

## Catching Database Errors Cleanly

Every database driver raises different low-level error codes when a unique constraint or foreign key fails. Repositories automatically translate native database errors across PostgreSQL, SQLite, MySQL, MariaDB, DuckDB, CockroachDB, Oracle, MSSQL, and Spanner into consistent Python exceptions:

```python
from advanced_alchemy.exceptions import DuplicateKeyError, ForeignKeyError, NotFoundError

async def safe_assign_role(
    db_session: AsyncSession,
    user_id: int,
    role_id: int,
) -> AdvancedUserRole | None:
    repo = AdvancedUserRoleRepository(session=db_session)
    try:
        return await repo.add(AdvancedUserRole(user_id=user_id, role_id=role_id), auto_commit=True)
    except (DuplicateKeyError, ForeignKeyError, NotFoundError):
        await db_session.rollback()
        return None
```

Source: https://docs.advanced-alchemy.litestar.dev/latest/usage/services.html

# Services

A **Repository** speaks in database tables (`BlogPost` rows), while a **Service** speaks in your API’s input and output shapes (`BlogPostCreate`, `BlogPostResponse`) and gives you one clean home for business rules—such as creating missing tags or generating URL slugs before saving.

## Setting Up a Service

Let’s connect a `BlogPost` table, Pydantic request/response schemas, and a `BlogPostService`:

```python
from sqlalchemy.orm import Mapped, mapped_column
from advanced_alchemy.base import BigIntAuditBase
from advanced_alchemy.mixins import SlugKey

class BlogPost(BigIntAuditBase):
    __tablename__ = "blog_service_post"
    title: Mapped[str] = mapped_column(index=True)
    content: Mapped[str]
    published: Mapped[bool] = mapped_column(default=False)

class BlogTag(BigIntAuditBase, SlugKey):
    __tablename__ = "blog_service_tag"
    name: Mapped[str] = mapped_column(unique=True, index=True)
```

```python
from pydantic import BaseModel

class BlogPostCreate(BaseModel):
    title: str
    content: str

class BlogPostUpdate(BaseModel):
    title: Optional[str] = None
    content: Optional[str] = None
    published: Optional[bool] = None

class BlogPostResponse(BaseModel):
    id: int
    title: str
    content: str
    published: bool
    model_config = {"from_attributes": True}
```

```python
from advanced_alchemy.repository import SQLAlchemyAsyncRepository
from advanced_alchemy.service import SQLAlchemyAsyncRepositoryService

class BlogPostService(SQLAlchemyAsyncRepositoryService[BlogPost]):
    class Repo(SQLAlchemyAsyncRepository[BlogPost]):
        model_type = BlogPost

    repository_type = Repo
```

## Creating, Updating, and Returning Schemas

Pass dictionaries, Pydantic models, `msgspec` structs, dataclasses, `attrs` classes, or `SQLModel` objects straight into `create` and `update`, then call `to_schema` to format the response:

```python
async def create_post(service: BlogPostService, payload: BlogPostCreate) -> BlogPostResponse:
    post = await service.create(data=payload, auto_commit=True)
    return service.to_schema(post, schema_type=BlogPostResponse)

async def update_post(service: BlogPostService, post_id: int, payload: BlogPostUpdate) -> BlogPostResponse:
    post = await service.update(data=payload, item_id=post_id, auto_commit=True)
    return service.to_schema(post, schema_type=BlogPostResponse)
```

## Adding Custom Business Rules

Need to auto-generate a unique URL slug whenever a tag is created or renamed? Override `to_model` (or `to_model_on_create` / `to_model_on_update`):

```python
from advanced_alchemy.repository import SQLAlchemyAsyncSlugRepository
from advanced_alchemy.service import ModelDictT, is_dict_with_field, is_dict_without_field, schema_dump

class BlogTagService(SQLAlchemyAsyncRepositoryService[BlogTag]):
    class Repo(SQLAlchemyAsyncSlugRepository[BlogTag]):
        model_type = BlogTag

    repository_type = Repo

    async def to_model(self, data: ModelDictT[BlogTag], operation: Optional[str] = None) -> BlogTag:
        dumped = schema_dump(data)
        if is_dict_without_field(dumped, "slug") and is_dict_with_field(dumped, "name"):
            dumped["slug"] = await self.repository.get_available_slug(dumped["name"])
        return await super().to_model(dumped, operation)
```

## Using Pydantic, Msgspec, Dataclasses, attrs, or SQLModel

Services work with all five major Python schema libraries—normalizing partial updates (ignoring unset fields automatically) and converting rows into response schemas:

```python
class BlogPostPatch(BaseModel):
    title: Optional[str] = None
    published: Optional[bool] = None

def as_pydantic(service: BlogPostService, post: BlogPost) -> BlogPostResponse:
    return service.to_schema(post, schema_type=BlogPostResponse)
```

```python
import msgspec

class BlogPostStruct(msgspec.Struct):
    id: int
    title: str
    published: bool

class BlogPostStructPatch(msgspec.Struct):
    title: str | msgspec.UnsetType = msgspec.UNSET
    published: bool | msgspec.UnsetType = msgspec.UNSET

def as_msgspec(service: BlogPostService, post: BlogPost) -> BlogPostStruct:
    return service.to_schema(post, schema_type=BlogPostStruct)
```

```python
from dataclasses import dataclass
from advanced_alchemy.utils.dataclass import Empty, EmptyType

@dataclass
class BlogPostDataPatch:
    title: str | EmptyType = Empty
    published: bool | EmptyType = Empty

def dump_dataclass_patch(patch: BlogPostDataPatch) -> dict[str, object]:
    return schema_dump(patch)
```

```python
from attrs import define

@define
class BlogPostAttrs:
    id: int
    title: str
    published: bool

def as_attrs(service: BlogPostService, post: BlogPost) -> BlogPostAttrs:
    return service.to_schema(post, schema_type=BlogPostAttrs)
```

```python
from sqlmodel import Field as SQLField, SQLModel

class ArticleRow(SQLModel, table=True):
    __tablename__ = "service_doc_article_row"
    id: Optional[int] = SQLField(default=None, primary_key=True)
    title: str

class ArticlePublic(SQLModel):
    id: int
    title: str

class ArticleService(SQLAlchemyAsyncRepositoryService[ArticleRow]):
    class Repo(SQLAlchemyAsyncRepository[ArticleRow]):
        model_type = ArticleRow
    repository_type = Repo
```

# Read/Write Routing

As your app grows, most database traffic is reading data—loading feeds, search pages, and dashboards—while only a fraction is saving changes.

Read/write routing lets you add **Read Replicas** alongside your main **Primary Database** without rewriting your repository calls:

## How Your Own Changes Stay Fresh

Replicas take a few milliseconds to copy new data from Primary. What happens if a user creates a new blog post and your code immediately loads that post on the next line?

Advanced Alchemy solves replica lag automatically: as soon as a session writes data, subsequent reads in that transaction stay pinned to Primary until `commit()` or `rollback()` finishes:

## Setting Up Primary and Replica Pools

Define your `"default"` writer and `"read"` replica pools in `RoutingConfig` and pass it to `SQLAlchemyAsyncConfig` (or `SQLAlchemySyncConfig`):

```python
from advanced_alchemy.config import SQLAlchemyAsyncConfig
from advanced_alchemy.config.routing import EngineConfig, RoutingConfig, RoutingStrategy

config = SQLAlchemyAsyncConfig(
    routing_config=RoutingConfig(
        engines={
            "default": ["postgresql+asyncpg://user:pass@primary:5432/db"],
            "read": [
                EngineConfig(
                    connection_string="postgresql+asyncpg://user:pass@replica-1:5432/db",
                    weight=2,
                    name="replica-east",
                ),
                EngineConfig(
                    connection_string="postgresql+asyncpg://user:pass@replica-2:5432/db",
                    weight=1,
                    name="replica-west",
                ),
            ],
            "analytics": ["postgresql+asyncpg://user:pass@analytics:5432/db"],
        },
        routing_strategy=RoutingStrategy.ROUND_ROBIN,
        sticky_after_write=True,
    ),
)
```

```python
from advanced_alchemy.config.routing import RoutingConfig

cloud_sql_routing = RoutingConfig(
    engines={
        "default": ["postgresql+asyncpg://user:pass@primary-ip:5432/mydb"],
        "read": [
            "postgresql+asyncpg://user:pass@replica-1-ip:5432/mydb",
            "postgresql+asyncpg://user:pass@replica-2-ip:5432/mydb",
        ],
    },
)
```

```python
from advanced_alchemy.config.routing import RoutingConfig

pool_endpoint_routing = RoutingConfig(
    engines={
        "default": ["postgresql+asyncpg://user:pass@writer.db.internal:5432/mydb"],
        "read": ["postgresql+asyncpg://user:pass@reader-pool.db.internal:5432/mydb"],
    },
)
```

```python
from advanced_alchemy.config.routing import RoutingConfig

local_routing = RoutingConfig(
    engines={
        "default": ["postgresql+asyncpg://user:pass@localhost:5432/mydb"],
    },
    enabled=False,
)
```

## Choosing a Pool Manually

Most routes never need manual overrides. When a critical checkout check must read from Primary—or a slow report should run on an `"analytics"` replica—wrap the call in a context manager or pass `bind_group`:

```python
from typing import Any
from advanced_alchemy.routing import primary_context, replica_context, use_bind_group

async def run_targeted_queries(repo: Any, item_id: Any) -> tuple[Any, list[Any], int]:
    with primary_context():
        fresh_row = await repo.get(item_id)

    with replica_context():
        feed_rows = await repo.get_many()

    with use_bind_group("analytics"):
        report_count = await repo.count()

    return fresh_row, feed_rows, report_count
```

## Complete Runnable Example

```python
"""Runnable read/write replica routing example for Advanced Alchemy."""

import shutil
import tempfile
from pathlib import Path

from sqlalchemy import create_engine
from sqlalchemy.orm import Mapped

from advanced_alchemy.base import BigIntAuditBase
from advanced_alchemy.config import SQLAlchemySyncConfig
from advanced_alchemy.config.routing import EngineConfig, RoutingConfig, RoutingStrategy
from advanced_alchemy.repository import SQLAlchemySyncRepository
from advanced_alchemy.routing import primary_context, replica_context, reset_routing_context

__all__ = (
    "Article",
    "ArticleRepository",
    "main",
)

class Article(BigIntAuditBase):
    """Article model used to verify read/write replica routing."""

    __tablename__ = "routing_example_article"

    title: Mapped[str]

class ArticleRepository(SQLAlchemySyncRepository[Article]):
    """Synchronous repository for routed Article persistence."""

    model_type = Article

def main() -> None:
    """Execute a complete primary-write and replica-read routing workflow."""
    reset_routing_context()
    with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as tmp_dir:
        primary_db = Path(tmp_dir) / "primary.sqlite"
        replica_db = Path(tmp_dir) / "replica.sqlite"
        primary_url = f"sqlite:///{primary_db}"
        replica_url = f"sqlite:///{replica_db}"

        primary_init_engine = create_engine(primary_url)
        Article.metadata.create_all(primary_init_engine)
        primary_init_engine.dispose()
        shutil.copyfile(primary_db, replica_db)

        config = SQLAlchemySyncConfig(
            routing_config=RoutingConfig(
                engines={
                    "default": [EngineConfig(connection_string=primary_url, name="writer")],
                    "read": [EngineConfig(connection_string=replica_url, weight=2, name="reader-1")],
                },
                routing_strategy=RoutingStrategy.ROUND_ROBIN,
                sticky_after_write=True,
            ),
        )

        with config.get_session() as session:
            repo = ArticleRepository(session=session)
            created = repo.add(Article(title="Primary Write"))
            created_id = created.id
            sticky_read = repo.get(created_id)
            if sticky_read.title != "Primary Write":
                msg = f"Unexpected sticky read title: {sticky_read.title}"
                raise RuntimeError(msg)
            session.commit()

        shutil.copyfile(primary_db, replica_db)

        with config.get_session() as session:
            repo = ArticleRepository(session=session)
            with replica_context():
                replica_articles = repo.get_many()
                if len(replica_articles) != 1 or replica_articles[0].title != "Primary Write":
                    msg = f"Unexpected replica articles: {replica_articles}"
                    raise RuntimeError(msg)

            with primary_context():
                primary_article = repo.get_one(title="Primary Write")
                if primary_article.id != created_id:
                    msg = f"Unexpected primary article id: {primary_article.id}"
                    raise RuntimeError(msg)
```

See [routing](https://docs.advanced-alchemy.litestar.dev/latest/reference/routing.html) for the full routing API reference.

Source: https://docs.advanced-alchemy.litestar.dev/latest/usage/caching.html

# Caching

Imagine 500 visitors opening the same popular author page at the exact same second. Without a cache, your database runs the exact same `SELECT` query 500 times.

Advanced Alchemy integrates with [dogpile.cache](https://dogpilecache.sqlalchemy.org/) so repeated lookups come straight from memory or Redis—and whenever you save changes to a row, stale cache entries are cleared automatically when the transaction commits.

## Installation

```bash
uv add "advanced-alchemy[dogpile]"
```

```bash
pip install "advanced-alchemy[dogpile]"
```

```bash
pdm add "advanced-alchemy[dogpile]"
```

```bash
poetry add "advanced-alchemy[dogpile]"
```

## Quick Start

Pass `CacheConfig` to your database configuration and enable `auto_expunge=True` on cached repositories. Every `repo.get()` and `repo.get_many()` call uses the cache automatically—or pass `use_cache=False` to skip the cache for a specific query:

```python
from sqlalchemy.orm import Mapped
from advanced_alchemy.base import BigIntAuditBase
from advanced_alchemy.cache import CacheConfig
from advanced_alchemy.config import SQLAlchemySyncConfig
from advanced_alchemy.repository import SQLAlchemySyncRepository

class CachedAuthor(BigIntAuditBase):
    __tablename__ = "cached_author_example"
    name: Mapped[str]

class CachedAuthorRepository(SQLAlchemySyncRepository[CachedAuthor]):
    model_type = CachedAuthor

db_config = SQLAlchemySyncConfig(
    connection_string="sqlite:///:memory:",
    create_all=True,
    cache_config=CacheConfig(
        backend="dogpile.cache.memory",
        expiration_time=300,
        key_prefix="authors:",
    ),
)

with db_config.get_session() as session:
    repo = CachedAuthorRepository(session=session, auto_expunge=True)
    created = repo.add(CachedAuthor(name="Ada Lovelace"), auto_commit=True)
    cached_row = repo.get(created.id)
    fresh_row = repo.get(created.id, use_cache=False)
    assert cached_row.id == fresh_row.id
```

## Choosing a Cache Backend

```python
from advanced_alchemy.cache import CacheConfig

redis_cache = CacheConfig(
    backend="dogpile.cache.redis",
    expiration_time=3600,
    arguments={
        "host": "localhost",
        "port": 6379,
        "db": 0,
        "distributed_lock": True,
    },
    key_prefix="myapp:",
)
```

```python
from advanced_alchemy.cache import CacheConfig

memory_cache = CacheConfig(
    backend="dogpile.cache.memory",
    expiration_time=300,
)
```

```python
from advanced_alchemy.cache import CacheConfig

memcached_cache = CacheConfig(
    backend="dogpile.cache.memcached",
    expiration_time=3600,
    arguments={"url": ["127.0.0.1:11211"]},
)
```

```python
from advanced_alchemy.cache import CacheConfig

disabled_cache = CacheConfig(enabled=False)
```

## What Happens Behind the Scenes

- **Safe rollbacks**: Cache entries are only cleared *after* `commit()` succeeds. If a transaction rolls back, your cache stays untouched.
- **No cache stampedes**: If 50 requests miss the same uncached key at once, one query runs and shares the result with the waiting requests.
- **Columns only**: Cached rows store column values, not related tables. Call `session.merge(row)` first if you need to lazy-load relationships later.

```python
from typing import Any
from sqlalchemy import inspect
from advanced_alchemy.cache import CacheConfig, CacheManager, setup_cache_listeners
from advanced_alchemy.utils.serialization import decode_json, encode_json

def custom_serializer(model: Any) -> bytes:
    mapper = inspect(model.__class__)
    payload = {col.key: getattr(model, col.key) for col in mapper.columns}
    return encode_json(payload).encode("utf-8")

def custom_deserializer(raw: bytes, model_class: type[Any]) -> Any:
    return model_class(**decode_json(raw.decode("utf-8")))

cache_manager = CacheManager(
    CacheConfig(
        backend="dogpile.cache.memory",
        serializer=custom_serializer,
        deserializer=custom_deserializer,
    ),
)
setup_cache_listeners()
```

See [cache](https://docs.advanced-alchemy.litestar.dev/latest/reference/cache.html) for the full caching API reference.

Source: https://docs.advanced-alchemy.litestar.dev/latest/usage/cli.html

# CLI & Migrations

Whenever you add a column or create a new table in Python, your SQL database needs a migration script to apply that change safely.

Advanced Alchemy includes a terminal tool called `alchemy` (plus `litestar database` and `flask database` when using web frameworks) that wraps Alembic so you can create migrations, upgrade databases, and export seed data with one command.

## Installation

```bash
uv add "advanced-alchemy[cli]"
```

```bash
pip install "advanced-alchemy[cli]"
```

```bash
pdm add "advanced-alchemy[cli]"
```

```bash
poetry add "advanced-alchemy[cli]"
```

## Pointing the CLI at Your Database Config

Tell `alchemy` where your database config lives once in `pyproject.toml` (recommended), with an environment variable, or with `--config` on the command line:

```toml
[tool.advanced-alchemy]
config = "myapp.db:alchemy_config"
```

```bash
export ALCHEMY_CONFIG="myapp.db:alchemy_config"
alchemy upgrade head
```

```bash
alchemy --config myapp.db:alchemy_config upgrade head
```

Your config target can be a `SQLAlchemyAsyncConfig`, `SQLAlchemySyncConfig`, a list of configs for multiple databases, a framework plugin/extension, or a zero-argument factory function:

```python
from advanced_alchemy.config import SQLAlchemySyncConfig

alchemy_config = SQLAlchemySyncConfig(
    connection_string="sqlite:///:memory:",
)
```

## Common Flags

| Flag | What It Does |
| --- | --- |
| `-c`, `--config` | Import path (`myapp.db:alchemy_config`) to your config or app plugin. |
| `--validate-config` | Prints discovered configs and checks them before running a command. |
| `--bind-key` | Runs the command only for one named database bind key. |
| `--no-prompt` | Skips confirmation prompts in CI or automated scripts. |

## Adding Commands to Your Own Click App

Already have a custom project CLI built with Click? Attach Advanced Alchemy’s migration commands directly to your group:

```python
import click
from advanced_alchemy.cli import add_migration_commands, get_alchemy_group

alchemy_group = get_alchemy_group()

@alchemy_group.command(name="seed-reference")
@click.option("--env", default="dev", help="Target environment name.")
def seed_reference(env: str) -> None:
    click.echo(f"Seeding reference data for {env}")

add_migration_commands(alchemy_group)
assert "upgrade" in alchemy_group.commands
```

## Next Steps

- [CLI Command Workflows](https://docs.advanced-alchemy.litestar.dev/latest/usage/cli_commands.html) — Step-by-step commands for creating migrations, checking drift, and exporting fixtures.
- [cli](https://docs.advanced-alchemy.litestar.dev/latest/reference/cli.html) — Full list of `alchemy` commands and flags.

Source: https://docs.advanced-alchemy.litestar.dev/latest/usage/cli_commands.html

# CLI Command Workflows

Once [your config is connected](https://docs.advanced-alchemy.litestar.dev/latest/usage/cli.html), day-to-day schema changes follow the same commands whether you run `alchemy ...`, `litestar database ...`, or `flask database ...`.

## Everyday Migration Flow

1. **Set up migrations once** in a new project, generate a migration script from your models, and apply it: ```bash
alchemy init migrations
alchemy make-migrations -m "create blog tables"
alchemy upgrade head
```
2. **Undo the last migration** or **preview raw SQL** without touching the database: ```bash
alchemy downgrade -1
alchemy upgrade head --sql
```

## Checking Configs and Schema Drift in CI

Run `show-config` to confirm which databases were found, and run `check` in CI to catch model changes that are missing a migration file:

```bash
alchemy show-config
alchemy check
alchemy history --indicate-current
```

## Handling Parallel Git Branches

When two teammates create migrations on separate branches, merge both heads into one linear revision before deploying:

```bash
alchemy heads --verbose
alchemy merge heads -m "merge feature migrations"
```

## Adopting an Existing Database or Exporting Data

```bash
alchemy ensure-version
alchemy stamp head
```

```bash
alchemy dump-data --table "*" --dir ./fixtures
```

```bash
alchemy drop-all --no-prompt
```

> **Warning**: `drop-all` permanently deletes every mapped table in the target database. Only run it against disposable local or test databases.

See [cli](https://docs.advanced-alchemy.litestar.dev/latest/reference/cli.html) for every command flag.

Source: https://docs.advanced-alchemy.litestar.dev/latest/usage/database_seeding.html

# Database Seeding

When setting up a new environment or staging server, you often want starter rows—such as default roles, categories, or sample products—loaded from version-controlled `.json` or `.csv` files.

Advanced Alchemy’s `open_fixture` and `open_fixture_async` helpers locate and parse fixture files (including compressed `.gz` and `.zip` files) in one call.

## Writing a Fixture File

Store your seed files in a `fixtures/` folder. JSON keeps numbers and booleans typed automatically, while CSV files load every column as strings:

```json
[
    {
        "name": "Laptop",
        "description": "16GB RAM and 1TB SSD",
        "price": 999.99,
        "in_stock": true
    },
    {
        "name": "Smartphone",
        "description": "5G OLED display",
        "price": 699.99,
        "in_stock": true
    }
]
```

```text
name,price,in_stock
Widget,9.99,true
Gadget,19.99,true
```

## Loading Fixtures Into Your Database

Pick `open_fixture_async` for async apps or `open_fixture` for sync scripts:

```python
from pathlib import Path
from typing import Optional
from sqlalchemy import String
from sqlalchemy.orm import Mapped, mapped_column
from advanced_alchemy.base import UUIDBase
from advanced_alchemy.config import AsyncSessionConfig, SQLAlchemyAsyncConfig
from advanced_alchemy.repository import SQLAlchemyAsyncRepository
from advanced_alchemy.utils.fixtures import open_fixture_async

async_config = SQLAlchemyAsyncConfig(
    connection_string="sqlite+aiosqlite:///db.sqlite3",
    session_config=AsyncSessionConfig(expire_on_commit=False),
)

class AsyncProduct(UUIDBase):
    __tablename__ = "async_products"

    name: Mapped[str] = mapped_column(String(length=100))
    description: Mapped[Optional[str]] = mapped_column(String(length=500), default=None)
    price: Mapped[float]
    in_stock: Mapped[bool] = mapped_column(default=True)

class AsyncProductRepository(SQLAlchemyAsyncRepository[AsyncProduct]):
    model_type = AsyncProduct

async def seed_async_products(fixtures_path: Path = Path("fixtures")) -> None:
    async with async_config.get_session() as db_session:
        repo = AsyncProductRepository(session=db_session)
        rows = await open_fixture_async(fixtures_path, "products")
        await repo.add_many([AsyncProduct(**row) for row in rows], auto_commit=True)
```

```python
from pathlib import Path
from sqlalchemy import String
from sqlalchemy.orm import Mapped, mapped_column
from advanced_alchemy.base import UUIDBase
from advanced_alchemy.config import AsyncSessionConfig, SQLAlchemyAsyncConfig
from advanced_alchemy.repository import SQLAlchemyAsyncRepository
from advanced_alchemy.utils.fixtures import open_fixture_async

async_config = SQLAlchemyAsyncConfig(
    connection_string="sqlite+aiosqlite:///db.sqlite3",
    session_config=AsyncSessionConfig(expire_on_commit=False),
)

class AsyncProduct(UUIDBase):
    __tablename__ = "async_products"

    name: Mapped[str] = mapped_column(String(length=100))
    description: Mapped[str | None] = mapped_column(String(length=500), default=None)
    price: Mapped[float]
    in_stock: Mapped[bool] = mapped_column(default=True)

class AsyncProductRepository(SQLAlchemyAsyncRepository[AsyncProduct]):
    model_type = AsyncProduct

async def seed_async_products(fixtures_path: Path = Path("fixtures")) -> None:
    async with async_config.get_session() as db_session:
        repo = AsyncProductRepository(session=db_session)
        rows = await open_fixture_async(fixtures_path, "products")
        await repo.add_many([AsyncProduct(**row) for row in rows], auto_commit=True)
```

```python
from pathlib import Path
from typing import Optional
from sqlalchemy import String
from sqlalchemy.orm import Mapped, mapped_column
from advanced_alchemy.base import UUIDBase
from advanced_alchemy.config import SQLAlchemySyncConfig, SyncSessionConfig
from advanced_alchemy.repository import SQLAlchemySyncRepository
from advanced_alchemy.utils.fixtures import open_fixture

sync_config = SQLAlchemySyncConfig(
    connection_string="sqlite:///db.sqlite3",
    session_config=SyncSessionConfig(expire_on_commit=False),
)

class SyncProduct(UUIDBase):
    __tablename__ = "sync_products"

    name: Mapped[str] = mapped_column(String(length=100))
    description: Mapped[Optional[str]] = mapped_column(String(length=500), default=None)
    price: Mapped[float]
    in_stock: Mapped[bool] = mapped_column(default=True)

class SyncProductRepository(SQLAlchemySyncRepository[SyncProduct]):
    model_type = SyncProduct

def seed_sync_products(fixtures_path: Path = Path("fixtures")) -> None:
    with sync_config.get_session() as db_session:
        repo = SyncProductRepository(session=db_session)
        rows = open_fixture(fixtures_path, "products")
        repo.add_many([SyncProduct(**row) for row in rows], auto_commit=True)
```

```python
from pathlib import Path
from sqlalchemy import String
from sqlalchemy.orm import Mapped, mapped_column
from advanced_alchemy.base import UUIDBase
from advanced_alchemy.config import SQLAlchemySyncConfig, SyncSessionConfig
from advanced_alchemy.repository import SQLAlchemySyncRepository
from advanced_alchemy.utils.fixtures import open_fixture

sync_config = SQLAlchemySyncConfig(
    connection_string="sqlite:///db.sqlite3",
    session_config=SyncSessionConfig(expire_on_commit=False),
)

class SyncProduct(UUIDBase):
    __tablename__ = "sync_products"

    name: Mapped[str] = mapped_column(String(length=100))
    description: Mapped[str | None] = mapped_column(String(length=500), default=None)
    price: Mapped[float]
    in_stock: Mapped[bool] = mapped_column(default=True)

class SyncProductRepository(SQLAlchemySyncRepository[SyncProduct]):
    model_type = SyncProduct

def seed_sync_products(fixtures_path: Path = Path("fixtures")) -> None:
    with sync_config.get_session() as db_session:
        repo = SyncProductRepository(session=db_session)
        rows = open_fixture(fixtures_path, "products")
        repo.add_many([SyncProduct(**row) for row in rows], auto_commit=True)
```

```python
from pathlib import Path
from typing import Any
from advanced_alchemy.utils.fixtures import open_fixture_async

def parse_csv_product(row: dict[str, str]) -> dict[str, Any]:
    return {
        "name": row["name"],
        "price": float(row["price"]),
        "in_stock": row["in_stock"].lower() == "true",
    }

async def seed_from_csv(repo: AsyncProductRepository, fixtures_path: Path) -> None:
    raw_rows = await open_fixture_async(fixtures_path, "products")
    products = [AsyncProduct(**parse_csv_product(item)) for item in raw_rows]
    await repo.add_many(products, auto_commit=True)
```

## Safe Re-Runs Across Deployments

Use `upsert_many` instead of `add_many` when a seed script runs on every deployment so existing rows are updated cleanly without duplicate errors:

```python
from pathlib import Path
from typing import Any
from advanced_alchemy.utils.fixtures import open_fixture_async

async def seed_roles(role_service: Any, fixtures_path: Path) -> None:
    rows = await open_fixture_async(fixtures_path, "role")
    await role_service.upsert_many(match_fields=["name"], data=rows, auto_commit=True)
```

> **Tip**: Seed parent tables (like `Author`) before child tables (like `Post`), and consider [Polyfactory](https://github.com/litestar-org/polyfactory) when generating random test data in `pytest`.

Source: https://docs.advanced-alchemy.litestar.dev/latest/usage/frameworks/index.html

# Framework Integrations

Instead of manually opening, committing, and closing SQLAlchemy sessions inside every web route, Advanced Alchemy plugs directly into your web framework.

Each integration starts and stops database engines cleanly with your app, gives every incoming request its own session, and re-exports core models, repositories, services, and filters from one place.

## At a Glance

| Framework | Setup Class | Included Features | CLI Tool |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [Litestar](https://docs.advanced-alchemy.litestar.dev/latest/usage/frameworks/litestar.html) | `SQLAlchemyPlugin` | Automatic DI, [DTOs & filters](https://docs.advanced-alchemy.litestar.dev/latest/usage/frameworks/litestar_dtos.html), [session stores](https://docs.advanced-alchemy.litestar.dev/latest/usage/frameworks/litestar_sessions.html), and [file uploads](https://docs.advanced-alchemy.litestar.dev/latest/usage/frameworks/litestar_storage.html) | `litestar database` |
| [FastAPI](https://docs.advanced-alchemy.litestar.dev/latest/usage/frameworks/fastapi.html) | `AdvancedAlchemy` | Lifespan sessions, [Depends services & filters](https://docs.advanced-alchemy.litestar.dev/latest/usage/frameworks/fastapi_dependencies.html), and [file uploads](https://docs.advanced-alchemy.litestar.dev/latest/usage/frameworks/fastapi_storage.html) | `alchemy` |
| [Starlette](https://docs.advanced-alchemy.litestar.dev/latest/usage/frameworks/starlette.html) | `AdvancedAlchemy` | ASGI session middleware, sync & async sessions, and multi-database support | `alchemy` |
| [Flask](https://docs.advanced-alchemy.litestar.dev/latest/usage/frameworks/flask.html) | `AdvancedAlchemy` | Request-context sessions, sync/async bridge, and `jsonify()` service helper | `flask database` |
| [Sanic](https://docs.advanced-alchemy.litestar.dev/latest/usage/frameworks/sanic.html) | `AdvancedAlchemy` | `sanic-ext` dependency injection, `request.ctx` sessions, and multi-binds | `alchemy` |

## Choose Your Framework

Full plugin integration with DTOs, controller dependency injection, server-side session stores, file storage, and `litestar database` commands.

ASGI lifespan management, typed `Depends` providers for services and OpenAPI query filters, multi-binds, and multipart file storage.

Lightweight ASGI middleware that attaches sync or async sessions to `request.state` across single or multiple databases.

WSGI and async route sessions, `FlaskServiceMixin` JSON responses, and built-in `flask database` migration commands.

Automatic session injection with `sanic-ext`, lazy `request.ctx` sessions, and multi-database bind keys.

Full class, provider, DTO, store, and CLI signatures for all five framework packages.

Source: https://docs.advanced-alchemy.litestar.dev/latest/usage/frameworks/litestar.html

# Litestar Integration

Advanced Alchemy is built by the Litestar team and plugs into Litestar with a single `SQLAlchemyPlugin`. One plugin setup handles database connections, per-request sessions, JSON serialization, error responses, and `litestar database` CLI migrations.

## What’s Included for Litestar

| Feature | What It Gives You | Guide & API |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Plugin & Configs** | Starts engines on app startup, opens a session per request, and maps database errors to HTTP responses. | [API](https://docs.advanced-alchemy.litestar.dev/latest/reference/extensions/litestar/plugins.html) |
| **Service & Filter DI** | Injects services and ready-made search/pagination filters straight into controller routes. | [Guide](https://docs.advanced-alchemy.litestar.dev/latest/usage/frameworks/litestar_dtos.html) · [API](https://docs.advanced-alchemy.litestar.dev/latest/reference/extensions/litestar/index.html) |
| **SQLAlchemy DTOs** | Auto-generates request/response DTOs from your SQLAlchemy models and `@property` fields. | [Guide](https://docs.advanced-alchemy.litestar.dev/latest/usage/frameworks/litestar_dtos.html) · [API](https://docs.advanced-alchemy.litestar.dev/latest/reference/extensions/litestar/dto.html) |
| **Sessions & Stores** | Connects multiple databases and stores server-side user sessions or cache keys in SQL tables. | [Guide](https://docs.advanced-alchemy.litestar.dev/latest/usage/frameworks/litestar_sessions.html) · [API](https://docs.advanced-alchemy.litestar.dev/latest/reference/extensions/litestar/store.html) |
| **File Storage** | Streams `UploadFile` payloads to local disk or S3/GCS and cleans up orphaned files on delete. | [Guide](https://docs.advanced-alchemy.litestar.dev/latest/usage/frameworks/litestar_storage.html) · [API](https://docs.advanced-alchemy.litestar.dev/latest/reference/types.html) |
| **Database CLI** | Adds `litestar database make-migrations`, `upgrade`, and `dump-data` commands automatically. | [API](https://docs.advanced-alchemy.litestar.dev/latest/reference/extensions/litestar/cli.html) |

```

```
